cards.title: Above-the-fold hero formula for landing pages
cards.summary: A six-element hero section (benefit headline, USP sub-headline, two social proofs, CTA, risk reducers, complementary image) that captures the majority of visitors who never scroll.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning the topmost section of a product, offer or lead-capture landing page for paid traffic.
steps: Treat the above-the-fold area (visible without scrolling) as the make-or-break section: the source states a large share of users never scroll past it, so put 80–90% of early effort here.
Write one benefit-driven headline that answers 'why should I care?' and ties to the customer's dream outcome. Avoid stating who you are, what you do, jargon or vague phrasing.
Add a sub-headline that carries your USP — who you are and why you differ from competitors.
Include at least two forms of social proof above the fold (reviews, testimonials, featured-in) to build credibility and give a reason to scroll.
Place a clear, action-oriented CTA button that stands out visually.
Directly beneath the CTA, place FUD reducers (free trial, money-back guarantee, easy returns, warranty) to defuse online-purchase anxiety.
Add one image or video that complements the messaging and subtly communicates the offer.

Run A/B tests on the headline and on the FUD block separately — the source reports these two elements alone produced large lifts for agency clients, but treat those figures as case examples, not guaranteed results.
caveats: Conversion lifts cited (e.g., 80% from headline alone, 40–60% from FUD testing) are the source's agency case-study examples, not universal benchmarks.
Apply to landing pages for a specific offer; top-of-funnel ad scaling belongs elsewhere.

cards.title: Emotion-first copy and imagery using PAS
cards.summary: Use imagery and the Problem-Agitate-Solve framework to trigger the emotional decision first, then support it with logical proof.
cards.use_when: Writing landing page copy or selecting hero/PDP imagery for cold traffic that doesn't yet know your brand.
steps: Decide what emotion the visitor arrives with — frustration at a problem or desire for an end-state improvement — and make that the emotional anchor of the page.
Lead with imagery: choose photos/video of real people experiencing the outcome (e.g., a happy customer using the product) because visual processing is much faster than reading text.
Structure a section with Problem-Agitate-Solve: name the problem in the visitor's own terms, amplify the pain it causes, then present your offer as the clear way out.
Layer logical reinforcement after the emotional hook — value props, guarantees, specs, comparisons — so the visitor can rationalize a decision already made emotionally.

For a product page, test replacing generic product-only shots with lifestyle images showing the outcome state; the source reports a tanning brand saw conversion lift after revamping its hero to feature a happy person using the product.
For a service or course, test a PAS section quoting the visitor's actual described struggles — the source reports a 282% lift after adding such a section, treating it as a case example.
caveats: The source's numeric lifts come from agency client cases and are illustrative, not guarantees.
Emotional imagery must match the target buyer — a mismatch (e.g., imagery aimed at the wrong persona) can hurt trust.

cards.title: Long landing pages convert when every section earns its place
cards.summary: Page length isn't the conversion problem — unhelpful, padded sections and hidden content are; treat the page like a digital salesperson.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many sections a paid-traffic landing page should have and what content to compress or cut.
steps: Accept that cold traffic generally won't convert straight from the ad — the ad gets the click; the page must do the selling.
Build the page like a salesperson: multiple value props, multiple social proof sections, multiple objection-handling sections, and clear reasons you're the best fit.
Audit each section with one question: does it move the visitor closer to converting? If not, cut or rewrite it.

Never hide critical content (especially reviews) in carousels, accordions, drop-downs or tabs — the source's rule is 'what is hidden will not get seen', and such elements get low engagement, especially on mobile.
On mobile, expose reviews inline rather than in a swipe carousel so visitors are forced to consume them.
Test page length as an experiment rather than assuming shorter is better; the source argues there is no fixed optimal length.
caveats: 'Long pages are fine' only holds if sections add value — padding for length's sake still hurts.
Length guidance is the source's opinionated stance; it directly contradicts common 'shorter is better' advice, so validate with your own traffic.

cards.title: Write for scanners: descriptive, benefit-driven section headlines
cards.summary: Assume visitors read only headlines and bullet points, so make every heading communicate the benefit on its own.
cards.use_when: Restructuring landing page or PDP copy so skimmers understand the offer without reading body text.
steps: Assume people read roughly 20% of content and scan the rest; design for the scanner first.
Replace generic section headers ('How it Works', 'Our Services', 'What Makes Us Unique') with full benefit statements that communicate the point themselves (e.g., 'What makes us different is X').
Use headings and sub-headings, bullet points for main value props, and bold text emphasized especially in headlines.
Run the headline-only test: read only the headlines top to bottom — is the full value proposition still clear and persuasive?
Write as a reader, not a writer: identify the one thing someone must know at a glance and put it front and center.
Ensure the reading flow is clear — body text kept in close proximity to its headline so scanned headlines and supporting detail stay connected.
caveats: Benefit-driven headlines must remain specific and honest; overclaiming in headlines can increase bounce or distrust.
This is copywriting craft guidance; results depend on traffic quality and offer strength.

cards.title: Make social proof verifiable to overcome skeptics
cards.summary: Add quotes to 'featured on' logos and use reviews with real names, photos and platform sources so credibility can actually be checked.
cards.use_when: Auditing or upgrading the social proof on a landing page or PDP, especially for cold paid traffic.
steps: Identify weak-but-common proof: bare 'featured on' logo bars, anonymous reviews, and repeated/duplicated logos. Remove repeats — repeated logos erode trust.

For each featured-on logo, add a short quote or snippet from the actual publication or appearance to add a layer of credibility. The source's agency client reportedly saw a 38% lift from this one change.
For reviews, require a real name, a photo of the reviewer, and the source platform (Google, Trustpilot, etc.) so a visitor can independently verify it.
Prefer verifiable third-party review sources over testimonials that could easily be fabricated.
Place at least two forms of proof above the fold, and expose reviews inline rather than hidden in carousels.
Test proof variants — logo-only vs. logo-with-quote, anonymous vs. named review — as separate experiments.
caveats: The 38% lift is a client case example, not a benchmark.
Consumer skepticism toward standard proof formats is described as a current marketplace trend; re-evaluate as behavior changes.
Only use real, verifiable reviews and quotes — fabricating proof defeats the purpose and creates legal/reputational risk.

cards.title: Use visual hierarchy and reduce choice to drive the CTA
cards.summary: Guide the eye from headline to sub-headline to CTA with size, weight, color and proximity, and remove competing elements that cause analysis paralysis.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a landing page or product page layout when the CTA is getting lost or the page feels cluttered.
steps: Define the priority order of elements: headline first, sub-headline second, CTA third, everything else after.
Use font size, weight and color to create clear distinction: headline bold and prominent, sub-headline subdued, CTA button large and contrasting.
Keep the CTA in close proximity to the headline and value copy so the eye flows naturally top to bottom.
Cut or demote competing elements — too many buttons, links, texts and colors cause analysis paralysis, and the source's mantra is 'less is more' (too much choice equals no choice).
Audit for clashing colors and elements of equal visual weight competing for attention; fix by reducing contrast conflicts and establishing one clear focal point.
Test the restructured hierarchy against the original; the source reports a 64% conversion lift from a hierarchy redesign for one client.
caveats: The 64% lift is an agency case example, not a promise.
'Less is more' must not conflict with the long-page principle — sections can be many, but each must have a clear single focus.

cards.title: Follow Jakob's Law: familiar layouts beat creative reinvention
cards.summary: Users expect landing pages to look and function like other sites they use, so standard structures (one headline, close body copy, top social proof, CTA) convert better than clever deviation.
cards.use_when: Choosing a landing page layout, template or redesign direction, especially when balancing brand creativity against conversion goals.
steps: Apply Jakob's Law: because users spend most of their time on other sites, they expect your page to follow familiar patterns — deviating from standard structure forces them to relearn navigation and hurts conversion.

Adopt the source's baseline structure: one clear headline, body text in close proximity to the headline, social proof near the top, CTA button directly underneath, FUD reducers beneath the CTA, and an image or video.
Avoid the minimalist trap of headline-only pages with no body text and no CTA — minimalism that removes clarity removes action.
Avoid multi-headline hero sections, oversized social proof that overpowers the headline, and body copy that sits far from the headline.
Before shipping a novel layout, ask whether the creativity comes at the cost of clarity; if yes, revert to a standard pattern.
When the layout is unconventional, run an A/B test against a familiar-layout control rather than assuming the creative version wins.
caveats: Jakob's Law is a UX heuristic, not a conversion guarantee; some strong brands convert well with differentiated design.
This contradicts advice to stand out visually — the source frames it as a trade-off favoring clarity over creativity when conversions are the goal.

input.text:
07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of seven core conversion rate optimization (CRO) principles for designing high-performing landing pages, focusing on UX design, copywriting, and psychological triggers to maximize leads and sales. Not here. • Driving top-of-funnel traffic or scaling ad accounts -> 06-MEA • Automated email sequences and abandoned cart flows -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a data-backed, actionable framework for structuring landing pages, detailing exactly what elements belong "above the fold" and how to use visual hierarchy and behavioral psychology to increase conversion rates. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, CRO, landing page design, above the fold, copywriting, visual hierarchy, social proof, Jakob's law, UX design] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the 5-second rule and above the fold / ensuring the topmost section of the page immediately answers "why should I care?" using a benefit-driven headline, USP sub-headline, social proof, and a clear CTA; emotional decision making / leveraging imagery and the Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) copywriting framework to tap into customer frustrations or desires before rationalizing the purchase with logic; landing page length / debunking the myth that long pages hurt conversions, arguing instead that pages should act like a comprehensive digital salesperson, provided no crucial information (like reviews) is hidden in drop-downs or carousels; designing for scanners / structuring copy with descriptive headlines, bullet points, and bold text to accommodate the 80% of users who scan rather than read; authentic social proof / combating consumer skepticism by adding specific quotes to "featured on" logos and using verifiable reviews with real names, photos, and platform sources; visual hierarchy / guiding the user's attention toward the CTA using contrasting colors, font weights, and proximity while avoiding analysis paralysis; Jakob's law and simplicity / favoring familiar, standardized web design layouts over overly creative or minimalist structures that sacrifice clarity.

Look for.

The "Above the Fold" Formula: The mandatory elements for the hero section: a benefit-driven headline tying to a dream outcome, a USP sub-headline, at least two forms of social proof, a clear CTA, FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) reducers, and a complementary image.

FUD Reduction Placement: The highly effective tactic of placing risk-reversal elements (e.g., "free trial," "money-back guarantee," "easy returns") directly underneath the primary CTA button to instantly alleviate purchase anxiety.

Descriptive Scanning Headlines: The copywriting rule to abandon generic section headers (e.g., "How it Works" or "Our Services") in favor of full, benefit-driven statements, assuming the user will only read the headlines.

Jakob's Law in UX: The psychological principle that users spend most of their time on other websites, meaning they expect your landing page to look and function in a familiar, standard way rather than reinventing the wheel.

Skip. Plugs for the speaker's CRO agency, mentions of specific client results without the accompanying strategic context, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of landing page elements), 85% growth (advanced UX psychology, CRO testing methodologies, and copywriting frameworks). Volume. ~400 words.

Do you ever wonder why some landing pages convert as high as 15% while others barely struggle to get any leads or sales? Well, over my last several years of experience in conversion rate optimization and landing page design, I've spent thousands of hours studying more than 1,500 plus landing pages to find out what actually makes them convert. Across the best landing pages I've seen in those last several years, I've noticed some very consistent patterns. So today, I'll be sharing what I found and give you my seven most key learnings that you can apply to your own landing page to optimize your conversion rate and get more leads and sales than you've ever seen before. Starting with lesson number one, which is by far the most important, and that is what I call the 5-second rule. If you don't hook someone and make a strong first impression in the first 5 seconds of someone landing on your page, you've completely lost them. That is why the topmost area of any landing page, also known as the above the fold, is complete make orb breakak. This is a section that's immediately visible without having to scroll down. And it is the only section that statistically 60% of people will never even scroll past, but 100% of your users will see. You should be spending 80 to 90% of your efforts just on this one section when starting out. In order to nail down the above the fold, here's the proven formula. The very first thing is having an extremely benefit-driven and compelling headline that ties into the dream outcome of your end user. Do not simply explain who you are or what it is you do in your headline. I see this mistake being made all the time on landing pages. Also, please do not use jargon or vague text that makes people have to process what you're trying to say. This is absolutely killing your conversions and it's a complete waste of your headline and it's causing you to burn money down the drain. The only thing you need in your headline is why should I care? Right? That's it. That's all you need. Just one hard-hitting benefit that makes people say, "Take my money." This is a great example for a bookkeeping client where we're highlighting value and quantifying the value in the form of time save. Right? That is what people care about at the end of the day. Here's another example where in the before version of our client's page, they simply just explain who they are and what it is they do, which is a digital imaging technician course. Right? This adds no value to me as the end user. In the after version, we tied in the dream outcome of the enduser and what they actually care about, right? Which is effectively more income, being able to travel the world and network with highprofile creatives. We've easily seen conversion rate increases at our agency at upwards of 80% just by testing the headline alone. So, the next thing is your sub headline, right? Your sub headline is the opportunity to now explain who you are and what it is you do to achieve the results that you just mentioned in your headline. In the sub headline, you want to convey your USP and what makes your product or service different than any other competitor out there in the market. The next big thing is having social proof above the fold, right? Social proof is anything like reviews, testimonials, featured publications, anything that's going to build trust with customers. Whenever you look at the world's highest converting landing pages, you will always notice that they put social proof right at the very top of their page because psychologically 60% of people never scroll past a section. So you have to give them a reason and incentive to actually scroll down in the page and take action. And social proof is one of the ways you do that. Ideally, you want to have at least two forms of social proof above the fold. We've just AB tested this a lot and we found that the more credibility you build up front, the higher likelihood someone is to convert. Next, you need a clear benefit-driven call to action button that stands out on the page and is actionable. Right underneath the call to action, you need to reduce what I call FUDs, which are fear, uncertainty, doubts. Right? All of the anxieties and fears that people have around shopping online or reaching out about a service, you need to reduce all of that upfront above the fold. This could be anything like free trials or return policies or warranties. You'd be surprised, but we've seen conversion rate increases between 40 to 60% just by testing this one small thing. So, these small little changes really make a difference. The final thing you need is an image or video that complements your messaging and subtly conveys who you are and what it is you do. Here's a before and after for our education client where we incorporated all of these techniques and we saw a 132% lift in qualified leads and conversions. Here's another example for a client sold thrillers where we saw a 108% lift in qualified leads and conversions from just optimizing their above the fold. Now, having a strong above the fold is literally just the bare minimum and basic prerequisites of getting people to scroll down and engage and take action on your page. But even despite giving them all of these logical reasons that they should take action, there's still going to be a large percentage of people that are not yet convinced. That is why lesson number two is that people buy with emotion, not logic. We like to think as humans that we're logical decision makers, but the reality is is that people tend to make decisions with emotion first, then they rationalize it with logic. So when a person comes to your landing page, they're feeling something. Maybe they're frustrated by some deep rooted problem in their life, or maybe they're dreaming of an endstate improvement in their life. Whatever it may be, that is the feeling that you need to tap into on your page. One of the easiest ways you can do this is through the form of images. Right? As the saying goes, a picture is worth a thousand words. And this couldn't be more true for your landing page. The human brain processes images 60,000 times faster than text. We did this for education client who caters towards children where you can see scattered throughout the page are tons and tons of photos of smiling and happy children that really resonates with their target audience, which is parents, and really hits home. This was one of the many changes that we made on this client's landing page that took them from a 2.5% conversion rate to a 5% conversion rate on meta ads and basically book them out with leads. For this tanning e-commerce brand, we completely revamped their hero section in which the before barely had any emotional connection and in the after we featured a happy person smiling actually using their products which built that emotional connection and resulted in a massive lift in conversions. The other way you can build this connection is through the use of powerful messaging. For our coaching client, his prospects struggled with dizziness and having to go through multiple physical therapists and multiple specialists. And so we highlighted this on the page through the form of powerful copy using the problem agitate solve framework where we basically first called out the problem. Then we agitated it and really made people feel the problem and turned up the heat and then we presented the solution as a clear way out of their problem. This was one of the many changes that we made to the landing page that led to a 282% lift in conversions and leads. And we literally saw people convert right there and then just after seeing the section. That's how powerful it is. When you combine the emotional appeal through colors, images, design, and copy, and you combine that with the logical appeal, that is the winning recipe for conversions. Speaking of conversions, lesson number three is that a long landing page does not kill conversions. Bad structure does. There is so much debate online about what the perfect length for a landing page looks like and countless studies online claiming one thing or the other. I'm here to tell you that there is nothing wrong with a long landing page as long as every section is adding value and getting people one step closer to conversion. I think people tend to forget, right? Long gone are the days with Google ads and Facebook ads that you can just throw up an ad and you'll start generating leads. There's no world in today's day and age where someone who knows nothing about your business, nothing about your brand, and nothing about your offer is just going to magically click on your ad and convert straight away. The ad is simply just to get the click. At the end of the day, your landing page is what needs to do the selling. And you need to treat your landing page like it's a saleserson. This means you need to have multiple value props, right? Multiple social proof sections, multiple sections where you're addressing people's fear, uncertainty, objections, and multiple sections where you're explaining to the customer why you're the absolute best fit and best solution for their problem to get them over the edge to convert. Some of the best landing pages that we've ever created at our agency are multiple sections long with tons of value props, tons of social proof, and tons of case studies. Following this principle, you need to be very careful and conscious about what you're going to hide in a carousel on mobile and hide in drop-own menus because they'll statistically get very very low engagement rates. Basically following the notion that what is hidden will not get seen. That is why whenever you look at our landing pages on mobile, we always expose the reviews and we never hide them in a carousel or in a drop down because we want to force people to consume those reviews, right? We want them to see those. Lesson number four is that people don't read, they scan. People will only read 20% of the content on your website. The other 80% they just scan. So people are just skimming your page and are trying to look for answers quickly and efficiently. So the question is, how do you make sure that people get the information they need without getting lost in the noise? It starts with structuring your landing pages in a way that's easy to scan. You need to utilize things like headings and subheadings. Bullet points to highlight the main value props like these examples here and bolding text to emphasize certain items, especially for your headlines. Right? This is something I see brands messing up all of the time. They use generic headlines like here's what we do, what makes us unique, how it works, or our services.
